description: Golden fixtures for the Runbook Executor. Two halves are scored from one run: the legacy execution path (skip_approval=True, so destructive steps deterministically resolve to 'denied' at the HITL gate while non-destructive steps execute) and the read-only discovery pass that produces the candidate list and the routing decision. The five original cases are unchanged; the cases below cover the decision rules (AUTO_SELECT / CANDIDATES / NO_RUNBOOK / AMBIGUOUS / NOT_APPLICABLE) and the explainability of the score. RA-004 uses no LLM, so every expectation is exact.

cases.description: A payment-service incident with no specific fault tag selects the generic restart runbook; the safe drain step runs, the destructive restart is gated -> denied.
'paymentservice' normalizes to the same service as 'payment-service' and still selects the runbook.
An OOM incident selects the memory-leak runbook over the generic restart, because tag overlap outscores a service-only match. Its clear_fault step is destructive, so it is gated.
A database dependency outage selects the MySQL runbook, which clears the fault, waits on the datastore, then verifies the app.
A service with no matching runbook returns a clean 'no_runbook' outcome rather than guessing.

The §4 example: order-service / EcommerceOrderErrorRateHigh / SEV-2 with an error-rate signal. The specific HTTP-500 runbook and the generic restart are both applicable, so the executor returns candidates for an SRE to choose instead of auto-selecting, and the specific one ranks first.

A memory-saturation incident on order-service: the HTTP-500 runbook is contradicted by the failure category and drops to NOT_APPLICABLE. What survives is every runbook that genuinely could explain memory pressure on this service — the application heap leak, the two external-pressure runbooks (release-only and release-then-recycle), and the always-applicable generic restart. That is four applicable candidates, so the SRE chooses (§6 CASE 2), and the executor reports AMBIGUOUS rather than guessing. The point of the case: working-set-over-limit cannot tell you WHOSE memory it is, so the library deliberately offers all the plausible causes instead of auto-picking one. No exact top_candidate is asserted — the three specific runbooks tie on score and specificity, so first place is decided by the id tie-break, and pinning it would test alphabetical ordering rather than matching.
§24: a resolved incident blocks the mandatory incident_active prerequisite, so the matching runbook is refused rather than run.

The legacy hand-off carries only service + tags, so the incident's lifecycle cannot be verified and applicability is undeterminable (§6 CASE 4). The executor reports AMBIGUOUS rather than picking a runbook off a keyword — the exact behaviour the v0 selector got wrong. The legacy half still runs and still reports 'denied' at the gate.
§6 CASE 3 through the new contract: nothing covers the service, so the decision is NO_RUNBOOK and the incident routes to RCA.
The shipped library declares demo + production. An incident in 'staging' contradicts every candidate, so nothing is applicable and nothing runs.
